Blood's path through the heart and lungs.Right atrium: It houses the sinoatrial node, the heart's natural pacemaker, which sets the rhythm of each beat.
Blood's path through the heart and lungs.Tricuspid valve: Three flaps close to stop blood flowing backwards, and the name means 'three points'.
Blood's path through the heart and lungs.Right ventricle: Its wall is thinner than the left's because it only pumps blood the short trip to the lungs.
Blood's path through the heart and lungs.Pulmonary valve: Its snap shut helps make the 'dub' in the heart's 'lub-dub' sound, along with the aortic valve.
Blood's path through the heart and lungs.Pulmonary artery: It's one of the few arteries that carry oxygen-poor blood, reversing the usual rule.
Blood's path through the heart and lungs.Lung capillaries: The lungs' roughly 300 million air sacs are wrapped in capillaries where blood swaps carbon dioxide for oxygen.
Blood's path through the heart and lungs.Pulmonary veins: The only veins in the body that carry oxygen-rich blood, reversing the usual pattern.
Blood's path through the heart and lungs.Left atrium: It has a small pouch, the left atrial appendage, where clots can form in atrial fibrillation.
Blood's path through the heart and lungs.Mitral valve: Named for a bishop's mitre, it has two flaps, unlike the three of the tricuspid valve.
Blood's path through the heart and lungs.Left ventricle: The thickest chamber, it pumps blood around the whole body and has the toughest job in the heart.

Australia and New Zealand through histor.First Fleet arrives: Eleven ships carried about 1,400 people, roughly half of them convicts, to Botany Bay and then Sydney Cove.
Australia and New Zealand through histor.Treaty of Waitangi: Signed by the Crown and Māori chiefs, its English and Māori texts differ in meaning, which still shapes debates today.
Australia and New Zealand through histor.Eureka Stockade: Gold diggers in Ballarat rebelled over license fees and flew the Southern Cross flag; the fight lasted barely 15 minutes.
Australia and New Zealand through histor.Ned Kelly hanged: The bushranger fought police in homemade iron armor, and his last words are famously reported as such is life.
Australia and New Zealand through histor.Australian Federation: Six colonies became one nation on January 1, and Canberra was later built as a compromise between rivals Sydney and Melbourne.
Australia and New Zealand through histor.Gallipoli landing: Australian and New Zealand troops landed on the Turkish peninsula in a failed campaign, now remembered every April 25 on Anzac Day.
Australia and New Zealand through histor.Sydney Harbour Bridge opens: Nicknamed the Coathanger, it was opened when a man in military uniform slashed the ribbon with a sword before the official could.
Australia and New Zealand through histor.Sydney Opera House opens: Its Danish architect Jørn Utzon left the project in 1966 and never saw it finished, and it took 14 years instead of four.
Australia and New Zealand through histor.Mabo decision: The High Court overturned the idea of terra nullius, recognizing that Indigenous people held land rights before colonization.
Australia and New Zealand through histor.Sydney Olympics: Cathy Freeman lit the cauldron and then won gold in the 400 meters, in front of a home crowd.

Speed check: from sound to light.Speed of sound (sea level): Sound travels at about 1,235 km/h at sea level in cool air, and breaking this barrier produces a sonic boom.
Speed check: from sound to light.Earth's spin at the equator: Because Earth turns once a day, a person at the equator is moving about 1,670 km/h, though you feel nothing because everything moves together.
Speed check: from sound to light.Concorde: Concorde cruised at twice the speed of sound and crossed the Atlantic in under three and a half hours, until it retired in 2003.
Speed check: from sound to light.International Space Station: The ISS circles Earth about every 90 minutes, so its crew sees around 16 sunrises and sunsets each day.
Speed check: from sound to light.Apollo 10 coming home: Apollo 10 set the human speed record on its return from the Moon in 1969, and the record still stands today.
Speed check: from sound to light.Voyager 1: Voyager 1 was launched in 1977, and it is the most distant human-made object, now in interstellar space.
Speed check: from sound to light.Earth around the Sun: Earth travels around the Sun at about 30 kilometres every second, so we are all flying through space all the time.
Speed check: from sound to light.Parker Solar Probe (top): Parker Solar Probe flies through the Sun's atmosphere, and it is the fastest human-made object ever, protected by a carbon-composite heat shield.
Speed check: from sound to light.The Sun around the galaxy: The Sun orbits the Milky Way's center about once every 230 million years, a stretch sometimes called a galactic year.
Speed check: from sound to light.Light: Light travels about 300,000 km every second, and nothing with mass can ever reach that speed.

British businesses, by founding year.Lloyd's of London: Lloyd's of London began as a coffee house, where sailors and merchants arranged insurance for ships, and it grew into a famous insurance market.
British businesses, by founding year.Sotheby's: Sotheby's is among the world's oldest auction houses, and it began by selling books before moving into fine art and jewels.
British businesses, by founding year.Christie's: Christie's sold its first lot in London and was founded by James Christie, and it has handled famous collections.
British businesses, by founding year.Boots: Boots began as a herbalist shop in Nottingham, started by John Boot, and later grew into a national chemist chain.
British businesses, by founding year.John Lewis: John Lewis began as a draper's shop on Oxford Street, and it later became owned by its employees, who are called partners.
British businesses, by founding year.Sainsbury's: Sainsbury's began with a single dairy shop in Drury Lane, London, and it grew into one of Britain's biggest supermarket chains.
British businesses, by founding year.BP (Anglo-Persian Oil): BP began as the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, which struck oil in Persia in 1908, and it later became a global energy giant.
British businesses, by founding year.Virgin: Virgin began as a mail-order record business started by Richard Branson, and it spread into airlines, trains and space travel.
British businesses, by founding year.ASOS: ASOS began as As Seen On Screen, selling copies of celebrity outfits, and it later became a huge online fashion retailer.
British businesses, by founding year.Deliveroo: Deliveroo started in London with its founder delivering meals on a bike, and it grew fast before listing on the stock market.

Meryl Streep films by release.Kramer vs. Kramer: It won the actress her first Oscar, for Best Supporting Actress, as the mother in a custody battle.
Meryl Streep films by release.Sophie's Choice: She won Best Actress, learning Polish and German accents for the role of a Holocaust survivor.
Meryl Streep films by release.Out of Africa: She played the Danish author Karen Blixen, and mastered a Danish accent for the part.
Meryl Streep films by release.The Bridges of Madison County: Clint Eastwood both directed and co-starred in it, and Streep earned another Oscar nomination.
Meryl Streep films by release.Adaptation: Charlie Kaufman wrote it, and in it she played the author Susan Orlean.
Meryl Streep films by release.The Devil Wears Prada: Her character, Miranda Priestly, was widely thought to be inspired by Vogue editor Anna Wintour.
Meryl Streep films by release.Mamma Mia!: Streep sang ABBA songs in the movie, which became the top-grossing movie musical at that time.
Meryl Streep films by release.Julie & Julia: She played the chef Julia Child, in a film directed by Nora Ephron.
Meryl Streep films by release.The Iron Lady: Playing Margaret Thatcher won her a third Oscar.
Meryl Streep films by release.Little Women: She played Aunt March in Greta Gerwig's adaptation of the Louisa May Alcott novel.

Materials that shaped civilization.Bronze: Mixing copper with tin makes a metal harder than either, giving the Bronze Age its name and its weapons.
Materials that shaped civilization.Glass: Early glass was made in Mesopotamia and Egypt for beads and small vessels, long before clear window glass.
Materials that shaped civilization.Iron smelting spreads: The Iron Age brought cheaper tools and weapons because iron ore is far more common than tin.
Materials that shaped civilization.Roman concrete: Made with volcanic ash, it has lasted two millennia, and the Pantheon's dome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome.
Materials that shaped civilization.Vulcanized rubber: Charles Goodyear's discovery that heating rubber with sulphur made it durable came by accident, and he died in debt.
Materials that shaped civilization.Bessemer steel: Henry Bessemer's converter blew air through molten iron to make steel cheaply, fuelling railways and skyscrapers.
Materials that shaped civilization.Cheap aluminium: Hall and Heroult found the electrolysis method independently in 1886; before that, aluminium was prized like a precious metal.
Materials that shaped civilization.Bakelite plastic: Leo Baekeland's invention was the first fully synthetic plastic, used in telephones and radios.
Materials that shaped civilization.Nylon: DuPont's invention first became famous as stockings, which sold in vast numbers within days of going on sale.
Materials that shaped civilization.Graphene: Geim and Novoselov peeled it from graphite with sticky tape, and it is a single layer of carbon atoms.

Running races, by distance.Olympic sprint: Olympic sprinters cover this in under 10 seconds, and the 100 m champion is traditionally called the world's fastest human.
Running races, by distance.The mile: Roger Bannister first broke the four-minute barrier in 1954; the distance, based on the old 'mille passus', is 1,609 m and comes from Roman marching measure.
Running races, by distance.Parkrun: Founded in 2004 in London, this free weekly timed run is held in parks around the world and relies on volunteers.
Running races, by distance.Classic road race: This distance is a staple of city road racing, and its 10,000 m also features on the track in athletics at the Olympic Games.
Running races, by distance.Half marathon: It's exactly half the 42.195 km marathon distance, and it has become one of the most popular road races for recreational runners.
Running races, by distance.Marathon: The distance of 42.195 km came from the 1908 London Olympics, when the course was set from Windsor Castle to the royal box.
Running races, by distance.Comrades Marathon: South Africa's ultra between Durban and Pietermaritzburg changes direction each year, and has a hard 12-hour cutoff, with runners racing the clock.
Running races, by distance.Western States 100: It began in 1977 when Gordy Ainsleigh ran the Tevis Cup horse trail in under 24 hours after his horse went lame, and a 100-mile race was born.
Running races, by distance.Badwater 135: This 135-mile race in Death Valley starts in the lowest point in North America, at about 85 m below sea level, in July heat.
Running races, by distance.Spartathlon: Runners cover the roughly 246 km from Athens to Sparta, in Greece, tracing the route that Pheidippides is said to have run, and kiss a statue of Leonidas.

Star Wars films in in-universe story ord.The Phantom Menace: It introduced Darth Maul and a young Anakin Skywalker, and in 1999 was the first new Star Wars film in 16 years.
Star Wars films in in-universe story ord.Attack of the Clones: It was the first major film shot entirely on digital video, rather than film stock.
Star Wars films in in-universe story ord.Revenge of the Sith: It ends with Anakin's transformation into Darth Vader, bridging the prequels to the original trilogy.
Star Wars films in in-universe story ord.Solo: A Star Wars Story: It shows Han winning the Millennium Falcon from Lando Calrissian, and explains the Kessel Run in 12 parsecs line.
Star Wars films in in-universe story ord.Rogue One: Its rebels steal the Death Star plans, and it ends just moments before A New Hope begins.
Star Wars films in in-universe story ord.A New Hope: Day zero of the in-universe calendar: BBY and ABY count years before and after the Battle of Yavin.
Star Wars films in in-universe story ord.The Empire Strikes Back: It reveals I am your father, set three years after the Battle of Yavin.
Star Wars films in in-universe story ord.Return of the Jedi: Its working title was Revenge of the Jedi, changed because Lucas decided Jedi don't seek revenge.
Star Wars films in in-universe story ord.The Force Awakens: Set about 30 years after the Death Star's destruction, it opens on the desert planet Jakku.
Star Wars films in in-universe story ord.The Rise of Skywalker: It ended the nine-film Skywalker saga, which took 42 years to make.

Printing and paper through history.Papyrus: It gave us the word paper, but papyrus is not true paper; it was made of pith from a Nile reed, laid in strips and pounded flat.
Printing and paper through history.Paper (China): Court official Cai Lun is credited with refining papermaking in 105 AD from tree bark, hemp rags and old fishing nets.
Printing and paper through history.Diamond Sutra printed: Found in a sealed cave at Dunhuang in 1900, this Buddhist scroll is the oldest dated printed book and is now in the British Library.
Printing and paper through history.Movable type (Bi Sheng): Bi Sheng carved characters in baked clay; the system was not widely adopted because Chinese needs thousands of different characters.
Printing and paper through history.Gutenberg press: Johannes Gutenberg printed his Bible in Mainz, roughly 180 copies, of which about 49 survive in whole or in part.
Printing and paper through history.Lithography: Alois Senefelder in Bavaria invented printing from a flat stone, using the fact that grease and water repel each other.
Printing and paper through history.Rotary printing press: Richard Hoe's press wrapped type around a cylinder, so newspapers could print thousands of sheets an hour instead of hundreds.
Printing and paper through history.Linotype machine: Ottmar Mergenthaler's machine cast whole lines of type from molten metal at a keyboard; its name means line o' type, and it ruled newsrooms for decades.
Printing and paper through history.Offset printing: Ink goes from plate to a rubber blanket and then to paper, which is the offset in the name; it still prints most books and magazines.
Printing and paper through history.Xerox 914 photocopier: Weighing around 300 kg, it was the first commercially successful plain-paper copier, and its brand name became a verb.

Ancient Roman festivals through the year.Lupercalia: On this Roman festival, priests known as Luperci ran around the city with strips of goat hide, and it later became associated with Valentine's Day.
Ancient Roman festivals through the year.Terminalia: The last day of the old Roman year was set aside to honor the god of boundaries, and neighbors would share a meal at their shared border stones.
Ancient Roman festivals through the year.Matronalia: Roman women held this festival for Mars, and husbands gave them gifts, a bit like a Roman Mother's Day.
Ancient Roman festivals through the year.Feast of Anna Perenna: This festival of a minor goddess of the year was celebrated with picnics and plenty of wine, and was said to promise as many years as cups drunk.
Ancient Roman festivals through the year.Parilia: Shepherds purified their flocks with smoke at this spring festival, and it was also the traditional day of Rome's founding.
Ancient Roman festivals through the year.Floralia: This spring festival for the goddess of flowers was known for being wild, with theatrical shows and more.
Ancient Roman festivals through the year.Lemuria: Romans held this festival to appease ghosts of the dead, with a head of household throwing black beans over his shoulder at midnight.
Ancient Roman festivals through the year.Vestalia: Only women could take part in this festival honoring the hearth goddess, and the temple was opened for them.
Ancient Roman festivals through the year.Volcanalia: This festival honored the god of fire, and fish were thrown into the flames as offerings.
Ancient Roman festivals through the year.Saturnalia: Rome's best-known holiday was a week of feasting and gift-giving, when masters served their slaves and rules relaxed.

Stages of human life, by age.Newborn: A newborn has about 300 bones, many cartilage, which fuse as they grow into the 206 of adulthood.
Stages of human life, by age.Infant: Babies roughly double their birth weight by around five months of age, and triple it by their first birthday.
Stages of human life, by age.Toddler: The word comes from toddle, an unsteady walk, and toddlers' brains form new connections at an astonishing rate.
Stages of human life, by age.Preschooler: Children's vocabularies grow from a thousand words or so at three to several thousand by the time they start school.
Stages of human life, by age.Tween: Tween means between child and teen, and the brain's prefrontal cortex keeps maturing into the mid-20s.
Stages of human life, by age.Teenager: The word teenager only became common in the 1940s, and teenage body clocks run later, which is why they stay up late.
Stages of human life, by age.Young adult: People in their 20s reach peak strength and reaction speed, and bone mass peaks around age 30.
Stages of human life, by age.Middle age: Many in middle age are the sandwich generation, caring for both children and aging parents.
Stages of human life, by age.Senior: Germany under Bismarck set a pension age of 70 in 1889, later lowered to 65, an age many countries still use.
Stages of human life, by age.Centenarian: Centenarians are among the fastest-growing age groups, and the oldest verified person, Jeanne Calment, lived to 122.

The last 250 million years, in order.Triassic: It began right after the worst extinction ever, the Permian, and ended with another, while dinosaurs and mammals both first appeared in it.
The last 250 million years, in order.Jurassic: Named for the Jura Mountains, it saw Stegosaurus and Brachiosaurus, plus the first birds, such as Archaeopteryx.
The last 250 million years, in order.Cretaceous: Its name comes from Latin 'creta', chalk, and it ended with the asteroid impact 66 million years ago.
The last 250 million years, in order.Paleocene: The world began recovering from the asteroid impact, and mammals started to diversify.
The last 250 million years, in order.Eocene: It began as a hot greenhouse world, and early whale ancestors were moving to the sea.
The last 250 million years, in order.Oligocene: Global cooling set in, Antarctic ice sheets grew, and grasslands spread.
The last 250 million years, in order.Miocene: Apes diversified and grasslands expanded across continents, shaping the mammals that followed.
The last 250 million years, in order.Pliocene: Australopithecus 'Lucy' lived about 3.2 million years ago, during this epoch.
The last 250 million years, in order.Pleistocene: It was the era of the ice ages, with mammoths and sabre-toothed cats, and the rise of Homo sapiens.
The last 250 million years, in order.Holocene: The current warm interglacial since the last ice age, though some scientists propose a new 'Anthropocene' epoch.

European animals by weight.Common shrew: It must eat almost constantly, every few hours, to feed its racing metabolism, and rarely lives beyond about two years.
European animals by weight.Red squirrel: It hoards nuts for winter. Across Britain it has been largely displaced by the introduced grey squirrel.
European animals by weight.Pine marten: An agile climber once nearly gone from Britain. Its comeback is helping red squirrels by keeping grey squirrels in check.
European animals by weight.Red fox: The most widespread wild canid, found across the northern hemisphere and now thriving in cities.
European animals by weight.European badger: It lives in a sett, a large underground burrow system that can be used and enlarged for generations.
European animals by weight.Eurasian beaver: Hunted nearly to extinction in Europe, it has been reintroduced and its dams create new wetlands.
European animals by weight.Gray wolf: Wolves have returned to much of western Europe, including Germany, after being wiped out over a century ago.
European animals by weight.Wild boar: The wild ancestor of the domestic pig. Piglets are born with striped coats that help them hide.
European animals by weight.Brown bear: Europe's largest land carnivore, with strongholds in the Carpathian mountains and Scandinavia.
European animals by weight.European bison: Wiped out in the wild by 1927, it was rebuilt from zoo animals and is Europe's heaviest land animal.

Missions arriving at Venus.Mariner 2: The first spacecraft to successfully fly past another planet, in December 1962. It found Venus's surface blazing hot.
Missions arriving at Venus.Venera 4: It sent data from within Venus's atmosphere in 1967, though it was crushed before reaching the surface.
Missions arriving at Venus.Venera 7: The first probe to transmit from the surface of another planet, though its signal was faint and lasted only about 23 minutes.
Missions arriving at Venus.Venera 9: Sent back the first photos ever taken from the surface of another planet, in black and white.
Missions arriving at Venus.Pioneer Venus: NASA's orbiter and probes mapped the planet by radar, revealing its high plateaus and vast lowlands.
Missions arriving at Venus.Vega 1: The Soviet probe dropped a lander and a balloon into Venus's air, then went on to study Halley's Comet.
Missions arriving at Venus.Magellan: Radar-mapped about 98 percent of the surface before being deliberately plunged into the atmosphere in 1994.
Missions arriving at Venus.Venus Express: ESA's first Venus mission. It found signs of lightning and a huge double vortex at the south pole.
Missions arriving at Venus.Akatsuki: Japan's orbiter missed its first attempt in 2010, then finally entered orbit five years later.
Missions arriving at Venus.BepiColombo (flyby): Flew past Venus on its way to Mercury, using the planet's gravity to adjust course.

Units of angle.Arcsecond: Astronomers measure star positions with it, and the Moon spans about 1,800 of them across the sky.
Units of angle.Arcminute: A nautical mile is one of these along a meridian, which is how sailors tie distance at sea to latitude.
Units of angle.Gradian: Surveyors use it, and a right angle has exactly 100 of them. It is sometimes marked 'grad' on calculators.
Units of angle.Degree: The 360 in a circle probably traces to Babylonian counting in sixties, and a sixtieth of it is an arcminute.
Units of angle.Point of the compass: An old compass is divided into 32 points, each 11.25 degrees, and sailors learned to 'box the compass' by reciting them.
Units of angle.Radian: The angle where the arc equals the radius, so a full circle has 2 pi of them. It is the natural unit in calculus.
Units of angle.Sextant: A sixth of a circle. The navigation instrument has the same name because its arc spans that angle.
Units of angle.Right angle: Carpenters' squares set this angle, whose name comes from the Latin for 'upright', and it is the cornerstone of most construction.
Units of angle.Straight angle: Half a turn, a perfectly straight line. Two right angles side by side make one, which is why triangle angles sum to it.
Units of angle.Full turn: Some mathematicians prefer to measure this with tau, equal to 2 pi, a symbol that makes one turn simply one tau.

Agatha Christie novels, by publication.Mysterious Affair at Styles: Christie's first novel introduced Poirot, and she wrote it after a bet from her sister Madge that she couldn't.
Agatha Christie novels, by publication.The Murder of Roger Ackroyd: Its shocking twist split critics, who debated whether the narrator had played fair, and made her famous.
Agatha Christie novels, by publication.The Murder at the Vicarage: The first Miss Marple novel sets the elderly sleuth in the village of St Mary Mead.
Agatha Christie novels, by publication.Murder on the Orient Express: She was inspired by her own journeys on the train, and by the Lindbergh kidnapping case in the news at the time.
Agatha Christie novels, by publication.The A.B.C. Murders: A killer sends Poirot letters signalling crimes in alphabetical order, in a clever puzzle on the theme of motive.
Agatha Christie novels, by publication.Death on the Nile: Christie had visited Egypt, and the novel's steamer setting made it among her most popular adaptations on screen.
Agatha Christie novels, by publication.And Then There Were None: It is often called the best-selling mystery ever, with over 100 million copies, and ten strangers die one by one on an island.
Agatha Christie novels, by publication.Evil Under the Sun: She based the setting on Burgh Island in Devon, a hotel on a tidal island where she often stayed.
Agatha Christie novels, by publication.A Murder Is Announced: Miss Marple solves a death that was advertised in the newspaper's classifieds, which drew villagers to a party.
Agatha Christie novels, by publication.Curtain: Christie wrote it during the Blitz and locked it away for decades, as it was Poirot's final case.

Famous fossil beds by age.Ediacara Hills: Its fossils record strange soft-bodied creatures, some of the earliest complex life, found in South Australia.
Famous fossil beds by age.Burgess Shale: The Canadian Rockies site, found by Charles Walcott in 1909, gave us creatures like Anomalocaris from the Cambrian explosion.
Famous fossil beds by age.Rhynie chert: Hot-spring silica here preserved some of the oldest known land plants and tiny arthropods in astonishing detail.
Famous fossil beds by age.Mazon Creek: Fossils sit in ironstone nodules, and include the strange Tully monster, Illinois's official state fossil.
Famous fossil beds by age.Solnhofen limestone: This Bavarian quarry yielded Archaeopteryx, the famed feathered link between dinosaurs and birds.
Famous fossil beds by age.Yixian Formation: Chinese beds of volcanic ash and mud have produced many feathered dinosaurs, including Sinosauropteryx.
Famous fossil beds by age.Dinosaur Provincial Park: This Alberta badlands park is a UNESCO site, home to fossils of about 50 dinosaur species.
Famous fossil beds by age.Hell Creek Formation: This formation in Montana and the Dakotas holds Tyrannosaurus and Triceratops from the last days of the dinosaurs.
Famous fossil beds by age.Messel Pit: An old German oil-shale pit preserved even soft tissue, in early horses, bats and birds.
Famous fossil beds by age.La Brea Tar Pits: Asphalt seeps here trapped dire wolves and sabre-toothed cats, and millions of fossils lie in the middle of Los Angeles.

Loanwords, by how far from London they w.Yacht: Yacht comes from Dutch jacht, meaning hunt, because the first ones were fast ships used to chase pirates and smugglers.
Loanwords, by how far from London they w.Kindergarten: Kindergarten is German for children's garden, a term created by Friedrich Froebel in 1837 for his early learning approach.
Loanwords, by how far from London they w.Paprika: Hungarian paprika comes from a Serbian word for pepper, and its pepper plants came from the Americas.
Loanwords, by how far from London they w.Vodka: Vodka literally means little water in Russian, a diminutive of voda, which is water.
Loanwords, by how far from London they w.Igloo: Igloo comes from Inuit iglu, which means house of any kind, not just ones made of snow.
Loanwords, by how far from London they w.Shampoo: Shampoo comes from Hindi champo, meaning to press or massage. It arrived in Britain as a head massage in Indian-style baths.
Loanwords, by how far from London they w.Chocolate: Chocolate likely comes from the Nahuatl word xocolatl, which was a bitter drink made from cacao.
Loanwords, by how far from London they w.Tycoon: Tycoon comes from Japanese taikun, meaning great lord, a title used for the shogun, then it entered English in the 1800s.
Loanwords, by how far from London they w.Ukulele: Ukulele is Hawaiian for jumping flea, perhaps for how fingers dance across the neck. It came from the Portuguese machete.
Loanwords, by how far from London they w.Kangaroo (Guugu Yimithirr): Kangaroo was recorded in 1770 by Captain Cook's crew from the Guugu Yimithirr language, though the old story of it meaning I don't understand is a myth.

Premieres of famous classical works.Vivaldi's The Four Seasons: Violin concertos, each paired with a sonnet. They were published in Amsterdam in 1725, part of a set called The Contest between Harmony and Invention.
Premieres of famous classical works.Handel's Messiah: It premiered in Dublin in 1742. Audiences stand for the Hallelujah chorus, supposedly because King George II did.
Premieres of famous classical works.Mozart's Don Giovanni: Premiered in Prague in 1787. Mozart reportedly wrote the overture the night before.
Premieres of famous classical works.Beethoven's Ninth Symphony: Beethoven was nearly deaf and had to be turned around to see the audience's applause at the Vienna premiere. It ends with the 'Ode to Joy'.
Premieres of famous classical works.Bizet's Carmen: The first night was poorly received. Bizet died three months later, never knowing it would become a favourite.
Premieres of famous classical works.Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake: It flopped in Moscow in 1877. Only after a revival in 1895 did it become the best-loved ballet.
Premieres of famous classical works.The Nutcracker: Premiered in St Petersburg in 1892. It became a Christmas staple in America after Balanchine's 1954 staging.
Premieres of famous classical works.The Rite of Spring: Its pounding rhythms and Nijinsky's choreography allegedly provoked near-riots at the Paris premiere.
Premieres of famous classical works.Rhapsody in Blue: Gershwin wrote it in about a month and played piano at the premiere. It opens with a famous clarinet glissando.
Premieres of famous classical works.Ravel's Boléro: Ravel repeats one melody and a snare drum rhythm while the orchestra builds steadily louder. He called it an experiment.

From bush to teapot: black tea.Pluck two leaves and a bud: The classic pick is the bud and the top two leaves of the tea bush, Camellia sinensis. Fine teas are still hand-picked this way.
From bush to teapot: black tea.Spread leaves out to wilt: Withering softens the leaves and reduces moisture, making them pliable. It can take about 12 to 18 hours, often on long troughs.
From bush to teapot: black tea.Roll leaves to bruise them: Rolling breaks cell walls so that juices mix with air. This releases the flavour compounds, and twists the leaf into its familiar shape.
From bush to teapot: black tea.Let them oxidise and darken: Oxidation turns green leaves coppery brown and creates black tea's malty flavour. Green tea skips this step, and oolong stops partway.
From bush to teapot: black tea.Dry them with hot air: Firing stops the oxidation and dries the leaf to lock in flavour. The tea is now shelf-stable and ready to store.
From bush to teapot: black tea.Sort into grades: Grades such as Orange Pekoe describe leaf size and whole or broken leaf, not quality or flavour. Smaller broken leaves are often used in tea bags.
From bush to teapot: black tea.Taste-test at auction: Professional tasters slurp tea loudly to spread it across the palate. Auction houses in places such as Kolkata and Mombasa sell vast quantities.
From bush to teapot: black tea.Blend different teas: Many popular teas, such as English Breakfast, are blends of several origins. Blenders aim to keep the flavour the same year after year.
From bush to teapot: black tea.Pack into tea bags: Tea bags were popularised in the early 20th century. Many were made of silk or muslin, and are now paper or plant-based material.
From bush to teapot: black tea.Brew in a teapot: Black tea is best brewed with water just off the boil, for about three to five minutes. Warming the pot first is a classic British tip.

Alice in Wonderland, in story order.Alice follows the White Rabbit: Lewis Carroll was a mathematician named Charles Dodgson, and Alice's Adventures in Wonderland came out in 1865.
Alice in Wonderland, in story order.Down the rabbit hole: The story began on a boat trip in 1862, when Dodgson told it to Alice Liddell and her sisters.
Alice in Wonderland, in story order.\"Drink me\": The shrinking and growing resemble Alice in Wonderland syndrome, a real condition that distorts perceived size.
Alice in Wonderland, in story order.Swimming in a pool of tears: The Dodo in the pool is often read as Carroll himself, who stammered his surname as Do-do-Dodgson.
Alice in Wonderland, in story order.Advice from a Caterpillar: The Caterpillar's famous question is Who are you?, asked while he smokes a hookah on a mushroom.
Alice in Wonderland, in story order.The grinning Cheshire Cat: The phrase grin like a Cheshire cat was around before Carroll, so the cat's grin may be a play on it.
Alice in Wonderland, in story order.A Mad Tea Party: Mad as a hatter is old, perhaps from mercury used in hat-making that could harm hatters' health.
Alice in Wonderland, in story order.Croquet with the Queen: The Queen's croquet uses flamingos as mallets and hedgehogs as balls, and her cry is Off with their heads.
Alice in Wonderland, in story order.Who stole the tarts? A trial: The trial opens with a nursery rhyme about the Queen of Hearts and her tarts, dating from the 1700s.
Alice in Wonderland, in story order.Waking up on the riverbank: Carroll's sequel, Through the Looking-Glass (1871), is built like a game of chess.

The Hunger Games, in story order.Prim's name is drawn: Suzanne Collins's 2008 novel is set in Panem, a future North America.
The Hunger Games, in story order.Katniss volunteers: Katniss volunteers and starts her journey; the three-finger salute of respect is a famous gesture.
The Hunger Games, in story order.Train to the Capitol: District 12, in the book, is set in Appalachia, a coal-mining region.
The Hunger Games, in story order.The girl on fire: Katniss is called the girl on fire thanks to Cinna's costume, which is a fashion highlight.
The Hunger Games, in story order.Training score of 11: Katniss scores 11 out of 12 in training by shooting an arrow at the Gamemakers' apple.
The Hunger Games, in story order.Peeta's TV confession: Peeta is a baker's son, and his love confession shapes the games.
The Hunger Games, in story order.Bloodbath at the Cornucopia: The Cornucopia is the horn of plenty from Greek myth, symbolising abundance.
The Hunger Games, in story order.Rue dies: Rue whistles the mockingjay song, though mockingjays are fictional hybrids of jabberjays and mockingbirds.
The Hunger Games, in story order.Rule change: two can win: The rule change lets two win, which sets up the final choice.
The Hunger Games, in story order.The poison berries: Nightlock berries are fictional, but Katniss's bluff shows the Capitol cares more about a winner than rules.

Ireland through the ages.St. Patrick's mission: Born in Britain, he was kidnapped and enslaved in Ireland as a teenager, and later returned as a missionary.
Ireland through the ages.Book of Kells made: This illuminated gospel manuscript is now on display at Trinity College Dublin, and was likely begun on the island of Iona.
Ireland through the ages.Battle of Clontarf: Brian Boru defeated a Viking and Leinster alliance but was killed in his tent; he's remembered as Ireland's greatest high king.
Ireland through the ages.Norman invasion: Anglo-Norman knights landed in Wexford, beginning centuries of English involvement in Ireland.
Ireland through the ages.Great Famine begins: Potato blight killed about a million people and drove another million to emigrate, and the population never recovered.
Ireland through the ages.Easter Rising: Rebels seized the General Post Office in Dublin, and the execution of their leaders swung public opinion.
Ireland through the ages.Irish Free State: It was established after the War of Independence and the Anglo-Irish Treaty, with six northern counties staying in the UK.
Ireland through the ages.Republic of Ireland: Ireland formally left the Commonwealth, and the republic took effect on Easter Monday.
Ireland through the ages.Joins the EEC: Ireland joined with the UK and Denmark, and EU funds later helped fuel the Celtic Tiger boom.
Ireland through the ages.Marriage equality vote: Ireland became the first country to legalise same-sex marriage by popular vote, with about 62 percent in favour.
